narration.heading: Sinking to the Titanic
narration.text: The Titanic is down there. And you're sinking straight toward it.

narration.heading: Sunlight zone
narration.text: Only the top two hundred metres are the sunlight zone. Below that, the light fades fast.

narration.heading: 1,000 m down
narration.text: Past one thousand metres, sunlight can't reach at all. You're sinking through total darkness.

narration.heading: 3,800 m down
narration.text: Three thousand eight hundred metres down, the Titanic's bow rises out of the dark.

narration.heading: The pressure
narration.text: Down here, the water presses about three hundred and eighty times harder than at the surface.

narration.heading: The impact
narration.text: When it sank in 1912, the bow slammed into this seabed at about ten metres per second.

narration.heading: The stern
narration.text: The stern lies six hundred metres away, in water just one or two degrees above freezing.

narration.heading: The twist
narration.text: The twist? A rust-eating bacterium, Halomonas titanicae, is slowly eating the ship's iron.

narration.heading: Gone by 2037?
narration.text: Some scientists think it could be gone by 2037. Should we raise what's left, or let the ocean keep it?

skit.text: Iron-eating bacteria? Good thing I'm mostly aluminium. I think.

titles: What if you sank all the way down to the Titanic?
Sinking 3.8 km to the Titanic, and what's eating it
youtube.description: Sink from the surface of the North Atlantic through the sunlight, twilight and midnight zones to the wreck of the Titanic, 3,800 metres down, and meet the rust-eating bacterium slowly destroying it.

sources.claim: The wreck lies about 3,800 m (12,500 ft) down, in two main pieces about 600 m apart
The Titanic sank on 15 April 1912; the bow hit the bottom at about 20 knots (10 m/s)
Water at the wreck is about 1-2 °C; Mann and Kaur's analysis says the wreck will not exist by 2037
The upper 200 m is the sunlight zone; below 1,000 m sunlight does not penetrate
Pressure rises by one atmosphere for every 10.06 m (33 ft) of depth, so about 380 atm at 3,800 m
A new rust-eating bacterium found in the Titanic's rusticles was named Halomonas titanicae
